name: Motu
content:
TOK PISIN CULTURAL STORY 4 - The Name of the Stranger

One Gutpela avinun, a young stranger arrived at the village. Pita saw him standing near the kona. 'Halo,' Pita said. The stranger answered quietly. 'Halo.' Pita asked, 'Yu orait?' 'Mi orait.' Pita smiled. 'Wanem nem bilong yu?' The boy answered, 'Nem bilong mi Saki.' Pita introduced himself. 'Nem bilong mi Pita.' Mara came over. 'Nem bilong yu wanem?' 'Saki.' Mara asked, 'Hamas krismas bilong yu?' Saki answered, 'Niu pa Patlima Masat.' Pita smiled. 'Yu i gat faiv krismas?' Saki nodded. The three children began talking. They discovered that they all liked walking through the forest. Soon an elder called them. 'Yupela i mas kam.' They walked steret, turned rait, then turned lep, and reached a gathering of manmeri. The elder looked at Saki. 'Welkam long ples bilong mipela.' Saki smiled. 'Tenkiu.' That night Saki said, 'Gutpela nait.' Pita answered, 'Lukim yu tumora.' The stranger was no longer a stranger. He had a name, new friends, and a place among the people.

Words in the story: Nem - name; Nem bilong mi - my name is; Wanem nem bilong yu? - what's your name?; Hamas krismas bilong yu? - how old are you?; Krismas - years old; Niu pa Patlima Masat - I am 5 years old; Gutpela avinun - good afternoon; Gutpela nait - goodnight; Welkam - welcome; Tenkiu - thank you; Lep - left; Rait - right; Steret - straight; Manmeri - people.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pronouns
lessons.content:
TOK PISIN CULTURAL STORY 1 - The Morning at the Village

Early one Gutpela monin, Pita woke up beside his family's house. He looked outside and saw many manmeri walking along the village path. Pita's friend Mara came to visit him. 'Halo, Pita!' Pita smiled. 'Halo, Mara. Yu orait?' 'Mi orait,' Mara said. 'And yu?' 'Mi orait.' Soon Pita's mother came outside. 'Yupela i go we?' Mara answered, 'Mipela i go long narapela sait bilong ples.' Pita looked at the people gathering near the path. Ol were carrying food and baskets. An old man named Toma was standing near the corner. 'Gutpela monin,' he said. 'Gutpela monin,' Pita answered. Toma smiled. 'Welkam. Yumi olgeta i mas wok bung.' Pita asked, 'Toma, wanem nem bilong yu?' The old man laughed. 'Nem bilong mi Toma.' Then he pointed toward the path. 'Go steret, na bihain tanim long rait.' Pita thanked him. 'Tenkiu!' Toma waved. 'Gutbai.' Pita and Mara began to wokabaut. They did not know yet that their small journey would teach them something they would remember for many years.

Words in the story: Mi - I/me; Yu - you; Em - he/she/it; Mipela - we; Yupela - you all; Ol - they/them; Halo - hello; Gutpela monin - good morning; Yu orait? - how are you?; Welkam - welcome; Tenkiu - thank you; Gutbai - goodbye; Nem bilong mi - my name is; Wokabaut - walk; Steret - straight; Tanim - turn; Rait - right.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Greetings
lessons.description: Greetings and polite phrases in Tok Pisin.
lessons.content:
TOK PISIN CULTURAL STORY 2 - The Path to the Other Side

After the morning gathering, Pita and Mara continued to wokabaut. They reached a kona where two paths separated. Mara looked left. 'Lep?' Pita looked right. 'Rait?' They were not sure. A group of manmeri came toward them. Pita politely said, 'Ekskius mi.' One woman stopped. 'Yu laik go long we?' Pita pointed ahead. 'Haus sik i stap long we?' The woman smiled and pointed down the path. 'Go steret. Bihain tanim long lep.' Pita thanked her. 'Tenkiu.' They followed her directions. They walked straight, turned left, and found the hospital. Inside, they met another group of people. 'Halo,' Pita said. 'Halo,' the people answered. Mara smiled. 'Gutpela avinun.' Everyone laughed. The two friends realized that sometimes the most important thing on a journey was knowing how to ask another person for help. That afternoon they began their journey home. 'Lukim yu tumora,' Pita said. 'Gutbai,' they replied. And Pita and Mara walked home.

Words in the story: Lep - left; Rait - right; Tanim - turn; Steret - straight; Kona - corner; Narapela sait - other side; Haus sik - hospital; Ekskius mi - excuse me; Manmeri - people; Wokabaut - walk; Halo - hello; Tenkiu - thank you; Gutpela avinun - good afternoon; Lukim yu tumora - see you tomorrow; Gutbai - goodbye.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Numbers
lessons.content:
TOK PISIN CULTURAL STORY 3 - The Twenty Gifts

One day, Pita and Mara were asked to help prepare food for a community gathering. An elder placed several baskets in front of them. 'Hamas?' Mara asked. The elder smiled. 'Yu mas countim.' Pita began. 'Wan. Tu. Tri. Foa. Faiv. Sikis. Seven. Et. Nain. Ten.' The children continued: 'Wanpela ten wan. Wanpela ten tu. Wanpela ten tri. Wanpela ten foa. Wanpela ten faiv.' They kept counting until they reached 'Tupela ten!' The elder nodded. 'Twenty.' One basket was almost empty. Pita looked at his own basket, then Mara's. 'Mipela i ken serim.' Soon the other children did the same. One gave food, another gave fruit, and another brought water. The baskets became full. The elder smiled. 'Gutpela.' Pita understood why a village was stronger when people helped one another.

Words in the story: Wan - one; Tu - two; Tri - three; Foa - four; Faiv - five; Sikis - six; Seven - seven; Et - eight; Nain - nine; Ten - ten; Wanpela ten wan - eleven; Wanpela ten tu - twelve; Wanpela ten tri - thirteen; Wanpela ten foa - fourteen; Wanpela ten faiv - fifteen; Tupela ten - twenty; Hamas - how much; Hamaspela - how many; Ol - they/them; Mipela - we.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Directions & Places
lessons.content:
TOK PISIN CULTURAL STORY 5 - The Way Home

The sun was going down. Pita, Mara and Saki had been walking for a long time. 'Mipela i mas go bek long ples,' Pita said. They reached a kona. 'Lep or rait?' Mara asked. Saki saw a group of manmeri. 'Let's ask them.' Pita called out, 'Ekskius mi!' An old woman pointed. 'Go steret. Do not turn there. Go to the narapela sait.' They thanked her. Soon they saw the lights of their village. 'Haus!' Saki shouted. Their families were waiting. Pita's mother ran toward them. 'Yupela i stap we?' Pita smiled. 'Mipela i kam bek.' The elder came forward. 'Gutpela nait, ol pikinini.' The children answered. The elder smiled. 'On a long road, you need more than directions. You need people.' The children looked at one another. Mi. Yu. Mipela. Ol. Different words, but together they had brought three children safely home. 'Lukim yu tumora,' the elder said. And everyone went home.

Capstone vocabulary: This story brings together vocabulary from all five Tok Pisin lessons: pronouns, greetings, personal information, numbers, directions and places.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Pronouns
lessons.content:
DUNA CULTURAL STORY 1 - The Beginning of the Journey

The morning was quiet. A young child named Kena stood outside his home. An elder approached him. 'Sirakura.' Kena bowed his head. 'Sirakura.' The elder asked, 'Koh paneme kay?' Kena answered, 'Noh paneme kay.' He pointed toward the mountain. 'Noh will walk there.' His friend Yali arrived. 'Koh are you going alone?' Kena shook his head. 'Anitiyah will go together.' Before they left, Kena asked the elder, 'Koh yakka ai?' The elder smiled. 'Noh yakka Toma.' He pointed toward the path. 'Walk carefully.' The children began walking past the trees, beside the garden, and toward the mountain. Behind them, the elder watched. The journey had begun.

Duna vocabulary used: Noh - I/me; Koh - you; Imane/Nane - he/she/it; Anitiyah - we; Sirakura - good morning; Koh paneme kay - how are you?; Yaka - name; Noh yakka - my name is; Koh yakka ai? - what's your name?; Raka - walk.

lessons.description: Learn daily greetings and polite phrases in Duna.
lessons.content:
DUNA CULTURAL STORY 2 - The Stranger by the Path

The children had walked for a long time. At midday they saw someone standing near the path. Kena called, 'Koh!' The stranger turned. Kena greeted him. 'Yopo.' The stranger replied, 'Yopo.' Kena asked, 'Koh paneme kay?' The stranger answered, 'Noh paneme kay.' Kena asked, 'Koh yakka ai?' The stranger replied, 'Noh yakka Mako.' Yali asked, 'Koh mali akita?' Mako smiled. 'Noh mali repu.' Five years old. The children sat together. Mako told them about a path on the other side of the mountain. He pointed toward the forest. 'Walk there.' The children thanked him. 'Suru kay.' Mako smiled. 'Sira kenda koneh.' See you tomorrow. The children continued their journey, repeating the directions as they walked. The forest became quiet. They knew they were no longer alone; they carried Mako's advice with them.

Duna vocabulary used: Yopo - good afternoon; Suru kay - thank you; Sira kenda koneh - see you tomorrow; Mali - years old; Noh mali repu - I am 5 years old; Koh mali akita? - how old are you?; Koh yakka ai? - what's your name?; Noh yakka - my name is; Raka - walk.

lessons.content:
DUNA CULTURAL STORY 3 - Counting at the Garden

The children reached a garden. An elder woman was preparing food. It was becoming night. She asked them to help. Kena began counting: 'Du. Yapa. Itupa. Sondopa. Repu.' The elder said, 'Keep going.' 'Raka. Kona. Fou. Key. Rapa.' They counted more: 'Repahne. Konane. Kinani. Mandi. Malura.' The elder laughed. 'Enough!' She pointed toward another basket. 'Akita?' They discovered there was enough food for everyone. The children helped carry it. They moved koyah and then sika, following the garden path. They raka until they reached the gathering place. The elder said, 'Food is not only for one person.' The children understood: they had counted the food, and now they had to share it. That night the garden became quiet. 'Akura,' the elder said. 'Akura,' the children answered.

Duna vocabulary used: Du - one; Yapa - two; Itupa - three; Sondopa - four; Repu - five; Raka - six; Kona - seven; Fou - eight; Key - nine; Rapa - ten; Repahne - eleven; Konane - twelve; Kinani - thirteen; Mandi - fourteen; Malura - fifteen; Akita? - how many/how much; Akura - goodnight; Koyah - left; Sika - right; Raka - walk.

lessons.content:
DUNA CULTURAL STORY 4 - The Path Through the Mountain

The next morning, Kena and Yali continued their journey. 'Sirakura,' they said. They reached a place where the path divided. Kena looked one way. Yali looked another. 'Koyah?' 'Sika?' They were uncertain. Then they saw an old man. 'Panah peh?' Kena asked. Where is the path? The old man pointed. 'Go ehtoto.' Straight. The children began to raka. After a while the man called, 'Pelani!' Turn. They reached another path. 'Kahanai,' the old man said. The other side. They crossed carefully and saw a building. Yali asked, 'Sick anda parama?' Where is the hospital? The old man pointed toward the Sick anda. The children thanked him. 'Suru kay.' They walked straight, turned, crossed to the other side, and walked again. Eventually they saw their home. They had found the way.

Duna vocabulary used: Koyah - left; Sika - right; Pelani - turn; Ehtoto / Seh - straight; Panah peh? - where is...?; Sick anda - hospital; Sick anda parama? - where is the hospital?; Raka - walk; Kahanai - other side; Suru kay - thank you; Sirakura - good morning.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Directions & Places
lessons.description: Navigate locations and ask for directions in Duna.
lessons.content:
DUNA CULTURAL STORY 5 - The Return

The sun was beginning to disappear behind the mountain. Kena and Yali had been travelling for many days. They had met people, learned names, counted food, and followed paths. Now they wanted to return home. Kena asked, 'Koh paneme kay?' Yali smiled. 'Noh paneme kay.' They began to raka. At a crossroads Yali remembered, 'Ehtoto.' Straight. Then, 'Pelani.' Turn. Soon they met Mako. 'Sira kenda koneh,' Mako said. Kena smiled. 'Suru kay.' At last they reached their village. Their families were waiting. An elder came toward them. 'Sirakura.' The children smiled. 'Sirakura.' The elder asked, 'Who are you?' Kena answered, 'Noh yakka Kena.' Yali introduced himself, 'Noh yakka Yali.' The elder smiled. 'Anitiyah.' We. The children understood that a journey is about the people encountered along the way, what others teach you, and knowing when to walk, turn, or ask for help. Night had arrived. 'Akura.' 'Akura,' the children answered. They entered their homes. The journey was finished, but the story would remain.

Duna capstone vocabulary: Noh - I/me; Koh - you; Anitiyah - we; Sirakura - good morning; Yopo - good afternoon; Akura - goodnight; Koh paneme kay - how are you?; Sira kenda koneh - see you tomorrow; Suru kay - thank you; Yaka - name; Noh yakka - my name is; Koh yakka ai? - what's your name?; Mali - years old; Du-Malura and higher numbers - counting; Akita? - how many/how much; Koyah - left; Sika - right; Pelani - turn; Ehtoto / Seh - straight; Panah peh? - where is...?; Sick anda - hospital; Raka - walk; Kahanai - other side.
